title: Crowley
name: Crowley
metaDescription: 1031 exchange coordination for Crowley, TX investors, where Chisholm Trail Parkway growth is bringing new retail construction that needs completion-stage documentation.

sections.html: Crowley sits along the Tarrant-Johnson county line south of Fort Worth, and its commercial base has changed quickly since the Chisholm Trail Parkway toll road opened a direct route between Crowley and the rest of Fort Worth. An exchange buyer here is often looking at newer construction rather than an established inventory, which shifts the documentation focus toward completion status and entitlement history.

sections.heading: How Chisholm Trail Parkway Changed Crowley's Commercial Base
sections.html:
Before the parkway opened, Crowley's commercial stock was limited mostly to older buildings along Crowley Road and the rail line running through town. Since the toll road connected Crowley to south Fort Worth, retail, service, and light industrial development has expanded along the new corridor, much of it recently built or still under construction.

That growth pattern means a larger share of Crowley's available inventory is new enough that final certificates of occupancy, recorded plats, and utility easements may not yet be fully documented at the county level, which changes what a title search will and will not turn up.

The surrounding school district and municipal infrastructure have generally expanded alongside this corridor growth, which is one indicator of how quickly the surrounding land use is shifting away from its historically rural character.

sections.heading: Property Types Available In Crowley
sections.html:
Crowley's trading stock reflects a market still catching up to its recent population and traffic growth.

  • newly built retail pads and small strip centers near the parkway corridor
  • light industrial and flex buildings on the town's rail-adjacent side
  • older retail and service buildings along historic Crowley Road
  • land parcels recently rezoned from agricultural to commercial use

Sorting a candidate into one of these categories early helps determine which documentation gap is most likely, since new parkway-corridor construction and older Crowley Road buildings carry almost opposite sets of open questions.

sections.heading: Where A Generic Exchange Scope Misses Crowley
sections.html:
A quote built for an established Fort Worth submarket assumes a finished title history, which is not always accurate for property built in the last few years along the parkway corridor. A properly scoped Crowley diligence list confirms whether the final plat has been recorded, whether the certificate of occupancy has actually been issued rather than only applied for, and whether any recent rezoning from agricultural to commercial use has cleared all required hearings.

It should also confirm which utility districts or municipal utility district assessments, if any, apply to the parcel, since newer development on the edge of Crowley sometimes carries district-level obligations that an older, established property would not.

sections.heading: Coordination Sequence For A Crowley Candidate
sections.html:
Once a Crowley property is under contract, the identification file should confirm the recorded plat status, final certificate of occupancy, and any municipal utility district assessment before the lender's underwriting proceeds. The qualified intermediary should be notified as soon as the purchase agreement is signed so funds are positioned ahead of the 45-day identification deadline.

For a property still finishing construction, the identification file should include a written completion timeline from the builder or developer, since the exchange's 45-day and 180-day deadlines do not adjust for a construction delay, and an investor needs to know that risk before committing to the candidate.

sections.heading: What The Crowley Identification File Should Contain
sections.html:
A complete file documents the recorded final plat, a current certificate of occupancy, any municipal utility district assessment history, and a title commitment confirming the rezoning process, where applicable, has fully closed out. Assembling this before the deadline avoids a delay caused by paperwork still moving through the county or city at the time of closing.

Where a property is still under construction, the file should also carry the builder's written completion date and any performance or completion bond in place, so the investor and the lender both have a documented basis for the closing timeline rather than an informal verbal estimate from the sales office.

faqs.q: Why does new construction in Crowley need different documentation than an established Fort Worth property?
faqs.a: Recently built parcels along the Chisholm Trail Parkway corridor may not yet have a fully recorded plat or final certificate of occupancy, so confirming both directly with the county or city is a necessary step before identification, and that step can take longer than a standard title search would suggest.

faqs.q: What changed in Crowley's commercial market recently?
faqs.a: The Chisholm Trail Parkway toll road opened a direct connection between Crowley and south Fort Worth, driving new retail, service, and light industrial development along the corridor in a way older Crowley Road frontage never supported.

faqs.q: Do municipal utility district assessments apply to Crowley properties?
faqs.a: They can on newer development at the edge of town. Confirming whether a parcel carries a district assessment is part of a properly scoped diligence list here, since the obligation can affect the property's net operating income.

faqs.q: What kinds of properties are available to buy in Crowley?
faqs.a: Newly built retail pads and strip centers near the parkway corridor, light industrial and flex buildings on the rail-adjacent side of town, older retail buildings on historic Crowley Road, and recently rezoned land parcels waiting on final commercial entitlement approval.

faqs.q: Should a rezoning from agricultural to commercial use be confirmed before identification?
faqs.a: Yes. Confirming that the rezoning process has fully closed out, including all required public hearings and final city council approvals, avoids an unresolved land-use question surfacing during lender underwriting later in the exchange.
